html:
The public supply of cheap and later free grain to the citizens of Rome. It began in 123 BCE with a law of Gaius Gracchus that let every citizen in the city buy a monthly ration of wheat at a fixed low price.

Rome had grown into a huge city fed by grain from overseas. Gracchus, like his brother Tiberius, courted the urban poor. Later politicians competed to make the ration cheaper, and in 58 BCE Clodius made it free. Julius Caesar cut the list to 150,000 people, and under Augustus about 200,000 men received free grain. Emperors ran the supply through an official, the prefect of the grain supply, and later added oil, wine and pork.

Feeding Rome tied the empire together. Fleets carried grain from Sicily, North Africa and above all Egypt, after Augustus took it from Cleopatra. The satirist Juvenal mocked a people who wanted only "bread and circuses". When Constantinople became the new capital, Egypt's grain went there instead.
sum: The public supply of cheap and later free grain to the citizens of Rome. It began in 123 BCE with a law of Gaius Gracchus that let every citizen in the city buy a monthly ration of wheat at a fixed low price.
